title: Hope
hookLine: hope is the virtue that trusts God to keep his promises
tomorrow: why would the risen Christ keep his scars?

cards: Fingers crossed. That emoji does a lot of work: the job offer, the test results, the text you're waiting on. That's wishing, and it runs on the odds.
Christian hope is a different thing, and the New Testament says it doesn't run on odds at all. One is a mood about how things might go. The other is a decision about whom to trust.

teach.h: HE IS FAITHFUL THAT HATH PROMISED.
teach.b: The letter to the Hebrews says to hold fast to hope, "for he is faithful that hath promised." Wishing asks, will it work out? Hope asks, will he keep his word?
Paul names it among three: "And now there remain faith, hope, and charity, these three." Hope is the one that leans forward.
Today's line is from Romans, in the Douay-Rheims: "And hope confoundeth not: because the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts." In that old English, confound means put to shame.
Hope doesn't leave you embarrassed for having had it, because it rests on love already given. And notice what comes just before, in Romans: tribulation works patience, patience trial, and trial hope.
Hope isn't what you have before trouble. It's what trouble can grow, when it's carried. Now look back at the week.
Prayer for the dead, the raised body, heaven, the saints, Mary at the hour, remembering death: each one makes sense only if somebody keeps promises past the grave. That's hope.
Hebrews gives it a picture: "an anchor of the soul, sure and firm."
Not a feeling that floats. A weight that holds.

how: Catholics count hope among the three theological virtues with faith and charity, and pray an act of hope; the anchor has long been a Christian sign of it.

o: feeling sure that things will turn out your way
a wish made on a candle, a star or a coin
trusting God to keep his promises, past the grave

games.q: the week, and the hope under it — tap the pairs.

s: it's trust in someone who keeps promises, not a mood.
Paul names faith, hope and charity together
and now there remain faith, hope, and charity, these three.
'hope confoundeth not' means hope doesn't confuse anyone
in that old English, confound means put to shame: hope doesn't leave you ashamed.

games.q: your teammate says "hope is for people who can't handle the odds." which reply fits today?
o: hope isn't about odds; it's trusting someone who keeps promises.
she's right; hope is a way to feel better about losing.
hope means expecting the best and ignoring the odds.
games.why: wishing runs on odds; hope, as Paul and Hebrews put it, runs on a promise-keeper.

practice: Say one hope out loud, quietly: something you can't make happen by yourself. Then say who you're trusting with it, a name, God's or someone's, and say it plainly, the way you'd hand over a key.
Let it settle the way an anchor settles, slowly, until it holds.

wordCard.voice: Hope. The virtue that trusts God to keep his promises, even past the grave. Not wishing: leaning on a promise.

orig.note: Greek: hope. the word Paul uses in Romans 5:5.

carryVoice: Your line: hope confoundeth not. It doesn't leave you ashamed for having hoped. Until tomorrow.
